classification.difficultyReason: Uses the supplied cases to classify triples by collinearity and centre inclusion, then explains the identity as a disjoint partition rather than numerical coincidence.

content.prompt: Nine points are drawn in the shape of an equal-armed cross as shown below.

spec.description: Nine black points in an upright equal-armed cross, with no connecting lines or labels.
spec.mathematics: Five horizontal and five vertical points share the centre. Two regularly spaced points lie beyond the centre on each arm.
spec.answerVisibility: The complete unlabelled point arrangement is permanently visible; no selected triples or triangles are shown.

children.prompt: Suppose three of the nine points are chosen.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many ways can this be done?

answer.worked:
Choose three points without regard to order:

$$\begin{align*}N&=\binom{9}{3}\\N&=84.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: How many ways can collinear points be chosen?

answer.worked:
A collinear triple must lie on the horizontal or vertical arm. Each contains five points, and no triple belongs to both.

$$\begin{align*}N&=2\binom{5}{3}\\N&=20.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: How many form triangles with the points chosen as vertices, and the middle point is one of the vertices?

answer.worked:
With the centre selected, choose one of the four other horizontal points and one of the four other vertical points. Choosing both on the same axis would give a line.

$$\begin{align*}N&=\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{1}\\N&=16.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: How many form triangles with the points chosen as vertices, and the middle point is

answer.short:

Choose the single vertex on one axis, then two vertices on the other axis.
answer.worked:
Without the centre, a triangle has two vertices on one axis and one on the other. Choose its single vertex from the eight noncentral points, then choose two of the four points on the other axis. Each triangle is counted once.

$$\begin{align*}N&=\binom{8}{1}\binom{4}{2}\\N&=8\times6\\N&=48.\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Every triple is either a triangle containing the centre, a triangle excluding the centre, or a collinear triple. These disjoint cases have counts $\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{1}$, $\binom{8}{1}\binom{4}{2}$ and $2\binom{5}{3}$, respectively.
answer.worked:
There are $\binom{9}{3}$ triples altogether. Subtracting the $2\binom{5}{3}$ collinear triples leaves all triangles. The triangles split into those containing the centre and those excluding it, counted in parts (c) and (d).

$$\begin{align*}\binom{9}{3}-2\binom{5}{3}&=\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{1}+\binom{8}{1}\binom{4}{2}\\\binom{9}{3}&=\binom{4}{1}\binom{4}{1}+\binom{8}{1}\binom{4}{2}+2\binom{5}{3}.\end{align*}$$
